title: Dual-scale investigation of temperature-dependent plasticity and damage of DP780
abstract: Accurate prediction of temperature-dependent plastic deformation and damage in advanced high-strength steels is essential for structural integrity under thermomechanical loading. This study presents a dual-scale, hybrid experimental–numerical approach to model plastic deformation and damage evolution in dual-phase 780 (DP780) steel from room temperature to 300 °C. Tensile tests with various geometries were conducted to investigate the effects of temperature and stress states. The results reveal a peak in strength and ductility at 300 °C due to dynamic strain aging (DSA), confirmed by serrated flow in nanoindentation tests on ferrite. Post-mortem microstructural analysis under scanning electron microscope (SEM) identifies martensite breakage as the dominant damage mechanism across all conditions. A temperature-dependent crystal plasticity model was calibrated using nanoindentation and representative volume element (RVE) simulations, enabling the extraction of phase-specific fracture strength thresholds. These microscale failure criteria were used to derive homogenized strain values under various stress states for calibrating a macroscopic continuum damage model. The calibrated model was verified by macroscopic tensile tests at different temperatures. This method enables accurate prediction of macroscopic fracture under multiple stress states and temperatures using physically grounded, microstructure-informed parameters. By bridging experiments, micromechanics, and continuum modeling, the proposed framework and the findings contribute directly to mechanical sciences by offering a novel, scalable path to link micro-scale damage to macro-scale failure, enhancing the reliability of damage modeling in dual-phase steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Dual-phase (DP) steel is one of the most widely used advanced high-strength steels (AHSS), especially in the automotive industry, due to its attractive combination of good formability and high strength [ 1–6 ]. DP steels typically contain a soft ferritic matrix with hard martensitic islands dispersed within it [ 5 , 7–10 ]. Comprehensive mechanical characterization and related microstructural analysis are essential for optimizing their design and enhancing their performance in structural applications [ 11–14 ].

Numerous micro- and macro-scale studies have been conducted on various types of DP steels to gain a profound understanding of their mechanical behaviors and the corresponding damage mechanisms [ 15 ]. The mechanical performances of steels, including the degree of plastic deformation and fracture points, are significantly influenced by damage mechanisms. Tasan et al. [ 16 ] performed Nakajima tests under various strain paths and SEM analysis, revealing that martensite can plastically deform at high volume fractions due to ferrite/martensite (F/M) boundary shearing. Tang et al. [ 17 ] performed in-situ testing associated with microscopic DIC in an SEM to demonstrate how increasing martensite content shifts damage initiation from ferrite grain boundaries (F/F) to F/M interfaces and eventually to martensite cracking, depending on martensite distribution. Ma et al. [ 18 ] linked fracture strain with temperature and stress triaxiality through multi-geometry testing and finite element (FE) simulations. Vermeij et al. [ 19 ] used crystal plasticity (CP) simulations to show that habit plane slip enhances plastic anisotropy and delays martensite damage. Aydiner et al. [ 20 ] employed cohesive zone modeling and 3D representative volume element (RVE)-based CP to identify how martensite connectivity influences damage evolution. Tran et al. [ 21 ] used machine learning (ML) and crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) to quantify the phase-level mechanical response, illustrating the transition from ferrite localization to F/F decohesion with increasing martensite content. Tseng et al. [ 22 ] used semi in-situ observation in SEM to explore the micro-damages in DP steels, finding out that interface decohesion comprises 52 % damage in DP780 necking and ferrite cracking comprises 67 % damage in DP980 necking. These studies, along with others [ 23–27 ], have identified three dominant ductile damage (nucleation) mechanisms in DP steels: decohesion at the F/F, decohesion along the F/M, and martensite cracking. The predominance of these mechanisms and the overall mechanical performances of steels can be influenced by the martensite volume fraction and distribution, local ferrite and martensite morphologies, and martensite hardness, etc. [ 28–31 ].

Characterizing mechanical properties and damage mechanisms is essential but insufficient. Increasing attention is now devoted to predicting mechanical performances directly from microstructural features. From a numerical perspective, the development of reliable, mechanism-based models that capture the microstructure and mechanical property relationship, especially under failure conditions, has become crucial. Such models provide not only deeper insight into deformation and fracture but also valuable guidance for material design and performance optimization. Such insights are not exclusive to DP steels, but also applicable to the majority of metallic systems. Among the multiple numerical approaches, including the FE method, extended FE method (XFEM), and fast Fourier transformation (FFT) method, the combination of CP and RVE approach has proven effective in capturing the microstructure-sensitive deformation and damage response of multiphase materials. Liu et al. [ 32 ] and Zhang et al. [ 33 ] applied the CP model and FFT to predict the macroscopic mechanical properties for aluminium alloys based on their microstructures. Jung et al. [ 34 ] proposed a dual-scale FE framework combining macroscale anisotropic plasticity and microscale dislocation-based CP to predict ductile fracture in DP steel. Results were validated via X-ray diffraction (XRD), nanoindentation, and RVE simulations coupled with focus ion beam electron back scatter diffraction (FIB-EBSD). Their damage predictions for DP steels aligned well with notched and hole expansion experiments. Zhang et al. [ 35 ] developed a damage-based CP model incorporating irradiation effects, temperature, composition, and microstructure, achieving accurate predictions of tensile responses in both neutron-irradiated and un-irradiated Zr-Nb specimens. Park et al. [ 36 ] generated an RVE comprising ferrite, martensite, and retained austenite for QP980 steels, incorporating deformation-induced martensitic transformation and transformation-induced plasticity effect in their novel CP model. Their model effectively captured the coupling between microstructural evolution and macroscopic mechanical response, highlighting the critical role of phase transformations. Liu et al. [ 37 ] developed a CP based virtual testing method for DP steels, validated by corresponding physical experiments. The resulting data enabled the calibration of phenomenological constitutive models, which were implemented into FE codes to simulate complex deformation and springback in U-bending processes of DP780 and DP980 sheets. The findings support the viability of virtual testing as a cost-effective alternative to conventional mechanical experiments in metal forming analysis. Similar approaches combining virtual testing and experimental validation have been reported by Qi et al. [ 38 ], Huang et al. [ 39 ], Ravi et al. [ 40 ], Meade et al. [ 41 ], etc. ML methods have also been extensively applied, since they can efficiently correlate microstructures and mechanical properties [ 42–45 ]. A typical example can refer to the work of Yoshihito et al. [ 46 ], who used generative adversarial networks (GANs) to generate DP steel microstructures and used FE modeling to predict tensile properties. Their results demonstrated that martensite volume fraction and morphology strongly influence strength and ductility. This study offers an efficient and accurate tool for predicting and optimizing the mechanical performance in DP steels.

However, many aforementioned studies focus on room temperature (RT), overlooking high-temperature behavior, which is critical for forming and service performance. The thermal-mechanical response of DP steels is complex and often non-monotonic [ 47 , 48 ]. Chandran and Verleysen [ 49 ] tested DP1000 steel from  
                         − 
                      40 °C to 400 °C using specimens with various geometries, revealing that dynamic strain aging (DSA) is closely associated with flow stress serrations, thermal hardening, and embrittlement. Decreasing temperatures can suppress DSA and its effects. To ensure the structural integrity of metallic components in the automotive, aerospace, and energy sectors, it is of critical importance to investigate the thermal mechanical behaviors of materials, especially fracture behavior at high temperatures. Developing more accurate models to capture thermal effects on mechanical performances for DP steels will contribute to their safety and integrity when applied in extreme environments with high temperatures [ 18 , 47 , 49 , 50 ]. Sen and Civek [ 51 ] conducted warm tensile tests on two types of DP steels and reported a significant improvement in deformability at 375 °C, attributed to reduced stress gradients between ferrite and martensite. Their work offers valuable insights for advanced automotive applications. Elevated temperatures can also induce microstructural changes, such as martensite tempering and ferrite softening, which influence crack initiation and propagation. Lapouga et al. [ 52 ] investigated steels containing over 80 % martensite subjected to laser heat treatment across a wide temperature range, demonstrating that strength degradation at elevated temperatures correlates with the formation of new austenite and the dissolution of the original martensite lath. Yan et al. [ 53 ] conducted elevated temperature tests on several types of cold-formed steels, including DP steel, finding that cold-formed DP steel exhibits relatively larger reduction in stiffness and strength than conventional cold-formed steels at high temperature. These studies underscore the importance of understanding temperature-driven microstructural evolution to optimize heat treatment processes for improved toughness and ductility without compromising strength—critical for both hot and cold forming applications [ 53–57 ]. Therefore, it is essential to identify the damage mechanisms at different temperatures and develop predictive numerical frameworks that incorporate microstructural features, temperature effects, and stress state dependence.

Aming to illustrate the microstructure and macroscopic mechanical property relationship of DP steels at elevated temperatures, so the structural integrity in practical applications can be guranteed, this study presents a hybrid experimental and numerical dual-scale investigation of the temperature effects on the plasticity and damage behavior of DP steels from room temperature to 300 °C.  Section 2  introduces the investigated DP780 material and experimental results. The material models are briefly summarized in  Section 3 . The calibration and validation procedures of material parameters are elaborated in  Section 4 . The damage prediction results considering the effects of temperature and stress state are presented in  Section 5 , followed by a summary of the main conclusions. By integrating experiments, micromechanics, and continuum modeling, this framework advances mechanical sciences by offering a scalable methodology that links microscale damage evolution to macroscale failure in DP steels and other steel materials.

sections.heading: Material and experiments
paragraphs: This section introduces the chemical composition and microstructure of the DP780 steel sheets with a thickness of 1.5 mm used in this study. It details the experiments to characterize micro- and macro-mechanical properties and to identify microdamage mechanisms. The mechanical properties between room temperature and 300 °C were obtained by performing nanoindentation (NI) tests and uniaxial tensile (UT) tests using different specimen geometries. Additionally, various characterization techniques, including SEM and EBSD, were employed to identify the damage mechanisms under different testing conditions.

sections.heading: Tensile tests between room temperature and 300 °C
paragraphs:
The uniaxial tensile tests were performed at four different temperatures, including RT, 100 °C, 200 °C, and 300 °C, using smooth dog bone (SDB) samples under the strain rate of 0.00025 s −1 . The sample geometry is shown in  Fig. 2 
                         . One optical extensometer with a gauge length of 50 mm was applied for the measurement of the longitudinal surface deformation in all tensile specimens. To evaluate the anisotropic effects, the SDB samples manufactured along 0

                          with respect to the rolling direction were tested at room temperature. The engineering stress-strain curves along different loading directions at RT are plotted in  Fig. 3 
                         (a), indicating that this DP780 steel can be assumed to be isotropic, particularly in the elastoplastic properties. Therefore, tensile tests at elevated temperatures were only performed along the rolling direction. Three parallel tests were conducted under each condition, and the results showed good repeatability.

The tensile properties of the DP780 steel at different temperatures along the rolling direction are shown in  Fig. 3 (b) and summarized in  Table 3 
                         , providing the average value and the corresponding standard deviation of each parameter. The average yield strength of this DP780 steel decreases slightly from RT to 100 °C, then increases at 200 °C, and slightly drops at 300 °C. In contrast, the average ultimate tensile strength shows the highest value at 300 °C. The average tensile strength increases with increasing temperature, particularly evident at 200 °C and 300 °C, which can be attributed to the DSA effect [ 58 , 59 ]. The DSA effect has been widely observed for ferritic and low-carbon steels and DP steels [ 60 , 61 ]. Average uniform elongation increases slightly from 19.0 % to 21.0 % when the temperature increases to 100 °C, then significantly decreases to 12.9 % at 200 °C and 13.2 % at 300 °C. The average total elongation follows a similar pattern to the uniform elongation. The temperature dependence of average yield strength and ultimate tensile strength is shown in  Fig. 3 (c), and the temperature dependence of average uniform and total elongation is shown in  Fig. 3 (d).

Fracture properties of the DP780 at different temperatures were investigated by carrying out tensile tests on samples with various geometries, including central-hole samples with a 3 mm radius hole (CHR3), notched-dog bone samples with a 10 mm radius notch (NDBR10), and plane-strain samples with a 3 mm radius notch (PSR3) samples, and shear (SH) samples. These samples were tested along the rolling direction at RT, 100 °C, 200 °C, and 300 °C, except that shear samples were tested only at RT. Good repeatability was obtained from three parallel tests, as evidenced in the force-displacement curves under different testing conditions in  Fig. 4 
                         . For a given sample geometry, at each temperature, good repeatability can be seen, and the highest tensile force is observed at 300 °C due to the DSA effects. The temperature effects on the fracture displacements of DP780 show a clear dependence on the stress state, which has been reported in other studies [ 59 , 62 ]. For CHR3 and NDBR10 samples, the fracture displacements are comparable at 200 °C and 300 °C, which are much larger than at RT and 100 °C. For PSR3 samples, the fracture displacements at 200 °C are comparable to those at 100 °C, which are much smaller than at RT and 300 °C. Overall, the highest fracture displacements are observed at 300 °C, indicating that the DSA might have positive impacts on the fracture properties under certain loading conditions.

sections.heading: Damage mechanisms from SEM analysis
paragraphs: The damage initiation mechanisms in the investigated DP780 during uniaxial tensile tests at different temperatures were revealed from the SEM analysis on the fractured smooth dog bone specimens. For each fractured sample, the fractured surface and the sub-surface near the fractured tip were observed. The sub-surface was prepared by cutting the fractured specimen in half lengthwise at a distance of 5 to 10 mm from the fracture surface, following the standard grinding, polishing, and etching (using Nital) procedures. The sub-surface was chosen to observe the deformation and damage evolution in both ferrite and martensite phases just prior to final failure, providing more relevant insight into phase-specific damage initiation.

Fig. 5 
                         (a) illustrates the fracture surfaces of specimens tested at temperatures ranging from RT to 300 °C. Across all samples, a mixed fracture morphology is observed, characterized by the coexistence of shallow, large dimples, quasi-cleavage facets, and river-patterned tear ridges. This fracture mode indicates the occurrence of martensite breakage. Similar observations were reported in [ 56 , 63 , 64 ]. Notably, with increasing temperature, the prevalence of cleavage features decreases, while the proportion of ductile dimples correspondingly increases.

Fig. 5 (b)–(e) presents the SEM images of the sub-surfaces from RT to 300 °C. As highlighted with yellow rectangles, martensite breakage is the dominant microscopic damage mechanism for the investigated DP780 steel from RT to 300 °C. Small voids can also be observed at the boundaries between ferrite and martensite. The same damage mechanisms were identified in other testing samples. It can also be seen that with increasing temperatures, the boundaries between martensite and ferrite become smoother and more blurred, especially at 300 °C. This can be attributed to the partial relief of residual stresses in martensite and the precipitation of fine carbides like ε-carbides or Fe₃C within the martensite laths or blocks [ 65–67 ]. This mild tempering effect under 300 °C causes the martensite boundaries to appear less distinct compared to their sharper appearance at RT [ 68–70 ]. Since 300 °C was not high enough, the ferritic grains did not experience significant grain growth or recrystallization.

Overall, considering the cleavage and quasi-cleavage features evident on the fracture surfaces in  Fig. 5(a) , together with the sub-surface martensite cracking observed in  Figs. 5 (b)–(e), and supported by the findings reported in [ 56 , 63 , 64 ], martensite breakage can be identified as the predominant microscale damage mechanism governing the failure behavior of the investigated DP780 steel over the entire tested temperature range.

sections.heading: Nanoindentation tests between room temperature and 300 °C
paragraphs:
To determine the temperature effects on the plastic flow behavior of ferrite and martensite phases, nanoindentation tests were performed using a Hysitron Triboindenter TI-980 instrument equipped with the xSol heating stage and a scanning probe microscopy (SPM). A thermal insulating tube connects the diamond Berkovich tip to a standard one-dimensional nanoscale dynamic mechanical analysis (nanoDMA) transducer, as shown in  Fig. 6 
                         (a). The transducer is covered with a special cylinder designed for high-temperature measurements. The set-up of the heating stage is shown in  Fig. 6 (b), featuring two heating rings (bottom and top) that ensure uniform temperature distribution across the sample. A thermocouple is positioned near the specimens to facilitate accurate and stable temperature control via a proportional-integral-derivative system. Additionally, protection gas (N 2  95 %, H 2  5 %) is used to maintain a safe and stable chemical environment during heating, avoiding any surface oxidation at high temperatures.

Nanoindentation tests were not performed for martensite due to the small grain size of martensite, making it challenging to precisely locate an indent within a single martensite grain using the Berkovich tip. The experimental force-displacement curves of nanoindentation tests at various temperatures are compared in  Fig. 7 
                         . The results indicate good repeatability for the nanoindentation tests performed at the same temperature. The averaged experimental force-displacement curves from parallel tests are compared in  Fig. 7 (e) for different temperatures. It is observed that although some variation in grain orientation exists ( Table 4 ), the overall shift in nanoindentation curves with increasing temperature consistently aligns with the temperature dependent macroscopic mechanical properties obtained from tensile tests.  Fig. 7 (f) compares the permanent displacement after complete unloading at different temperatures. It can be seen that the permanent indentation depth after unloading first increased when the testing temperature increased from RT to 100 °C. When the temperature further increased, the permanent displacement decreased, indicating that the material’s hardness increased at 200 °C and 300 °C. Moreover, the loading segments at 200 °C and 300 °C exhibited many serrations, especially at 200 °C, which are not visible on the macroscopic tensile stress and strain curves. The serrations in the force-displacement curves of nano-indentation tests, as well as the non-monotonic temperature dependence of permanent displacements, are evidence of the DSA on the microscopic scale. The motion velocity of solute atoms does not align with that of dislocation cores. Consequently, once the dislocation nucleation cores overcome the dragging force, a sudden displacement change appears in the load-displacement curve. The observed temperature impacts on the flow behavior of DP780 in nanoindentation tests correlate well with the macroscopic tensile test results. However, the different manifestations of the DSA in macroscopic tensile tests and nano-indentation tests need to be further investigated, which is out of the scope of this study.

sections.heading: Plasticity parameter calibration and validation
paragraphs: This section presents the methods used to calibrate the CP model parameters of ferrite and martensite, followed by the validation using experimental results. Various numerical approaches can be applied to solve the constitutive equations and calibrate the CP model parameters. These include the FE method with Gaussian integration points and the fast Fourier transformation (FFT) method, which uses regular Fourier points. Considering the complex boundary conditions, the CPFEM simulations of nanoindentation tests were performed to determine the CP parameters of ferrite using ABAQUS. Furthermore, the CPFFT method was applied in combination with an RVE to simulate uniaxial tensile tests using DAMASK, based on which the CP parameters of martensite were determined.

sections.heading: CP parameters of ferrite
paragraphs:
To calibrate the CP model parameters of ferrite in the DP780 steel, a three-dimensional FE model of nanoindentation test using a Berkovich indenter was constructed in ABAQUS. 4-node 3D rigid (R3D4) elements were used for the indenter, and 8-node 3D continuum (C3D8) elements were used for the grain. The finest meshes, with an element size of 30 nm, were applied to the critical deformation area (centre) of the grain, while coarser meshes were applied elsewhere. To improve convergence, the tip and three edges of the Berkovich indenter were slightly smoothed. To avoid penetration, the finest mesh at the tip of the Berkovich indenter had an element size of 50 nm, slightly larger than the ferrite grain size in the critical deformation area. The force-control mode was adopted, and the loading direction was along the z-direction. Friction between the tip and grain was neglected during the simulation to achieve better convergence. sections.heading: Scale bridging in damage prediction
paragraphs: To link microstructural features with macroscopic fracture response, a dual-scale framework was developed in this study, integrating CP simulations with RVEs. This section details the methodology for extracting phase-specific fracture strengths from CP simulations, determining stress-state-dependent damage initiation strains, and calibrating the continuum damage model at different temperatures. The validity of the calibrated model was subsequently assessed through comparison with experimental results.

sections.heading: Extraction of fracture strength from CP simulations using RVE
paragraphs:
As presented in  Fig. 5 , experimental observations consistently indicate that fracture in the investigated DP780 steel initiates predominantly through martensite breakage across all tested temperatures. Based on this, a stress-based failure criterion was employed to define the onset of damage based on CP simulation results. Specifically, CP simulations using the RVE were first performed under uniaxial tension conditions at different temperatures. Assuming the macroscopic uniform elongation is the onset of damage initiation, the maximum principal stress, i.e., the maximum eigenvalue of the Cauchy stress tensor, was computed for each grain in the RVE at the deformation level corresponding to the macroscopic uniform elongation of uniaxial tensile tests. The averaged maximum principal stresses in all martensite grains were taken as the critical fracture strength of martensite at each temperature. The maximum principal stress criterion is applied to describe the damage initiation in the brittle martensite phase. When the critical strength

sections.heading: Prediction of the fracture behavior at different temperatures
paragraphs:
In order to predict the fracture behavior during macroscopic tensile tests using the continuum damage model, the macroscopic flow curves need to be determined at different temperatures. Typically, the parameters in different phenomenological hardening laws can be optimized based on experimental true stress and strain curves obtained from uniaxial tensile tests. Alternatively, the flow curves up to high strain levels can be obtained from virtual uniaxial tensile tests using the CP model. As shown in  Fig. 11 , the CP simulation results agree well with the experimental results, particularly in the hardening phase. Therefore, both approaches should deliver similar results in the optimization of flow curve parameters. The Swift-Voce hardening law is employed in this study and the optimized parameters are summarized in  Table 11 
                         .

With the calibrated flow curves and damage initiation parameters, tensile simulations for various specimen geometries were conducted in ABAQUS. The MBW model was implemented via a user-defined VUMAT subroutine. Solid elements with reduced integration (C3D8R) are used in all models and symmetry boundary conditions along the thickness plane have been implemented.

The predicted force-displacement curves during tensile tests at different temperatures are compared with experimental ones in  Fig. 15–16 
                         
                         . The representative experimental results are shown as dotted curves and the simulation results are plotted as solid curves. The predictions of macroscopic fracture properties under the combined influence of stress state and temperature demonstrate very good accuracy, considering that the macroscopic damage criterion is derived from CP simulations. Minor deviations are observed under certain loading conditions, such as in the CHR3 specimens tested at 300 °C. These deviations can be mainly attributed to the non-proportional loading effects during tensile tests, whereas ideal proportional loading paths are applied in the CP simulations.

It is worth noting that this dual-scale framework is currently applicable within a temperature range where a dominant microscopic damage mechanism, e.g., martensite fracture, prevails. For regimes involving multiple competing mechanisms, e.g., ferrite rupture, phase transformation above ∼700 °C, different failure criteria, e.g., stress- or strain-based, may be required at the microscale. Additionally, phase transformation effects must be incorporated in such cases.

Despite the scale differences between the nanoindentation- and RVE-based microscale models and the macroscopic tensile simulations, the proposed method effectively predicts temperature- and stress-state-dependent fracture responses in DP steel. The framework is generalizable to other materials exhibiting microstructure-sensitive failure.

Furthermore, although damage evolution is not explicitly implemented within the CP framework, a stress-based fracture threshold is determined based on CP simulations via post-processing to identify damage initiation. These critical stress states are then linked to homogenized strain outputs, which serve as the basis for defining initiation loci in the continuum damage mechanics model.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This study develops a microstructure-informed framework to investigate temperature-dependent plastic deformation and damage behavior in dual-phase DP780 steel. By using a dual-scale hybrid experimental–numerical approach, the following key conclusions are drawn: 
                         
                            1. 
                            Temperature influence on plastic deformation and damage: Both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength increase with temperature up to 200 °C due to DSA, and subsequently decrease at 300 °C. Serrated flow observed in nanoindentation curves of ferrite confirms the occurrence of DSA at the microscale. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            Damage mechanism identification: SEM observations reveal that martensite cracking is the dominant damage initiation mechanism across all investigated temperatures. Cracks tend to initiate at the martensite phase and ferrite–martensite interfaces due to local stress concentrations. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            Crystal plasticity-based parameter extraction: Temperature-dependent CP parameters for ferrite and martensite are calibrated using nanoindentation and RVE simulations. Fracture strength thresholds for each phase are extracted and compared. The defined fracture criteria are used to calibrate the continuum damage model under different temperatures. The calibrated continuum damage model is successfully verified by macroscopic tensile test results. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            Dual-scale modeling framework: The proposed approach successfully bridges the microscale deformation behavior with macroscale fracture predictions, offering accurate and physically grounded damage evolution models under various loading conditions.

This work integrates dual-scale modeling, stress-state sensitivity, and temperature effects into a unified damage analysis strategy for dual-phase materials. This methodology can be extended to other AHSS and thermal loading scenarios, serving as a foundation for predictive structural design and materials development under complex thermomechanical conditions.
